title: Students’ perceptions of using ChatGPT in a physics class as a virtual tutor
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This study examines how undergraduate students perceive ChatGPT when it is used as a virtual tutor in a college physics course. The paper focuses on three questions: how accurate ChatGPT is at answering physics problems, whether students’ trust depends on the accuracy of the answers, and how trust influences their perceptions of ChatGPT’s usefulness, ease of use, and future use intentions.

The intervention was implemented in an introductory physics class at a public university in the southern United States. Forty students first completed a regular in-person exam, then used ChatGPT over about a week and a half to work through a makeup exam assignment based on questions they had answered incorrectly. Students interacted with ChatGPT using a structured prompt flow but could also ask follow-up questions. Quantitative data came from accuracy checks, trust classification, and a post-study Likert survey; qualitative data came from students’ drawings of how they تصور ChatGPT.

Results showed that ChatGPT answered physics questions with 85% accuracy overall, but many students still trusted its answers even when they were wrong. Trust level was associated with students’ perceptions: those who trusted ChatGPT more also rated it as easier to use and were somewhat more likely to intend to use it in the future. Drawing analysis suggested many students anthropomorphized ChatGPT or viewed it as a robot/machine, and some held misconceptions that it was infallible, magical, or super-intelligent. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can be error-prone in science contexts and that AI literacy, critical thinking, and prompt engineering are needed to reduce blind trust and misconceptions.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational/mixed-methods study with survey, dialogue-log, and drawing analyses, but it is not an experimental causal design and has a small, single-class sample. The evidence is useful for describing perceptions and risks, but it does not meet higher causal credibility thresholds.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a moderate accuracy problem (85% correct, with some answer instability) and substantial overtrust, but the study is limited to one undergraduate physics class and reports no direct learning outcome gains or harms for achievement. The practical impact is therefore important but still unclear and not yet generalizable.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a virtual tutor/assistant to answer undergraduate physics exam questions and support students in revising incorrect answers through dialogue

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered 85% of 362 physics questions correctly (307 correct, 55 incorrect) in an introductory college physics class (n=40). However, it sometimes changed answers after follow-up questioning, including 34 cases where a correct answer became incorrect and 7 cases where an incorrect answer became correct, indicating unstable scientific correctness despite generally high accuracy.
finding.measure: Accuracy of ChatGPT responses to physics questions; correctness of answers in an exam-makeup dialogue task

finding.finding_summary: Students showed strong trust in ChatGPT even when it was inaccurate: the Trust group agreed with ChatGPT 100% of the time, and nearly half of students accepted all answers regardless of correctness. Trust level was significantly related to answer accuracy, F(2,37)=6.383, p=0.004, η2=0.257, and also to perceptions of usefulness/ease of use/intention to use, indicating notable effects on critical evaluation and AI literacy-related judgment.
finding.measure: Trust/agreement with ChatGPT answers; perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and intention to use; drawing-based misconceptions about AI

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported favorable perceptions of ChatGPT as a learning aid, and the Trust group rated it higher on ease of use (M=4.34) than the Partial Trust group (M=3.65), with a significant group difference in overall perception, F(6,70)=2.478, p=0.031, η2=0.175. This suggests the tool was viewed as easy and potentially useful, although these perceptions were intertwined with overtrust and misconceptions.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use in the future
